questions.question: Using the potential energy versus internuclear distance graph, explain why two hydrogen atoms bond while two helium atoms do not, and define bond length and bond energy in terms of that graph.
questions.expected_answer: As two hydrogen atoms approach, each nucleus attracts the other atom's electron as well as its own, and by sharing both electrons each atom effectively completes its outer shell, so the potential energy falls. The energy reaches a minimum at the separation where this attraction balances the repulsion between the two positive nuclei — at smaller separations the energy climbs steeply. The separation at the minimum is the bond length, about 74 pm for hydrogen, and the depth of the minimum — the energy released when the bond forms, equal to the energy needed to break it — is the bond energy. Two helium atoms each already possess a filled shell of two electrons, so sharing lowers no energy: their curve shows no significant minimum, there is no hollow to settle into, and no bond forms. Bonding occurs because and only because it lowers energy.

questions.question: Predict and explain the shapes and approximate bond angles of methane, ammonia and water, given that each central atom is surrounded by four electron pairs.
questions.expected_answer: Electron pairs around a central atom repel one another and spread as far apart as possible; four pairs adopt the tetrahedral arrangement with angles of 109,5°. In methane all four pairs bond to hydrogens, so the molecule is tetrahedral with angles of 109,5°. In ammonia one of the four pairs is a lone pair; since a shape is named from the positions of the atoms only, the visible shape is a trigonal pyramid, and because the lone pair sits closer to the nitrogen and repels more strongly than bonding pairs, the H–N–H angle is squeezed to about 107°. In water two of the four pairs are lone pairs, leaving an angular or bent molecule, with the two lone pairs pinching the H–O–H angle further to about 104,5°. The electron arrangement is tetrahedral in all three molecules; the visible shape and the angle change only because lone pairs replace bonding pairs and push harder.

questions.question: Using electronegativity values (H 2,1; C 2,5; O 3,5; F 4,0; Cl 3,0; Na 0,9), classify the bonds H–F, Cl–Cl and Na–Cl, and then explain why carbon dioxide is a non-polar molecule while water is polar, although both contain polar bonds.
questions.expected_answer: Electronegativity measures an atom's tendency to attract the shared electron pair. Cl–Cl: difference 0, the pair is shared equally, non-polar covalent. H–F: difference 4,0 − 2,1 = 1,9, so the pair sits strongly toward fluorine, which becomes δ− while hydrogen becomes δ+; a very polar covalent bond. Na–Cl: difference 3,0 − 0,9 = 2,1, large enough for essentially complete electron transfer, forming ions; an ionic bond. Bond character slides continuously from equal sharing through unequal sharing to transfer as the difference grows — there is no sharp wall. Molecular polarity needs both polar bonds and a shape that fails to cancel them. Carbon dioxide is linear: its two equal C=O bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and cancel, so the molecule is non-polar. Water is angular: its two O–H dipoles lean toward the same oxygen side and add, leaving the oxygen end δ− and the hydrogen side δ+, so water is a polar molecule.
